title: The Sharpest Thing in Nature
outline:
The book opens on the boiling point, because everything difficult about the subject is already present there. Josiah Willard Gibbs supplied the framework of thermodynamic potentials and coexistence in 1878, Paul Ehrenfest supplied the classification in 1933, and Lev Landau supplied the order parameter and the language of symmetry breaking in 1937. The chapter establishes precisely what a first-order transition is, why latent heat implies a discontinuous first derivative, and why modern usage retains Ehrenfest's first-order category while replacing his second order with the word continuous, since real continuous transitions diverge as power laws rather than jumping by a finite amount. It then states the problem the rest of the book answers. A neural network is a smooth differentiable interpolator. A phase transition is a singularity in the thermodynamic limit. Finite systems have no true singularities at all, only rounded crossovers that sharpen with size, which means that every machine learning result in this field is inferring an idealization from data that does not contain it.

Built on Gibbs on heterogeneous equilibrium, Ehrenfest's 1933 Amsterdam classification with Tilman Sauer's 2016 translation and commentary, Landau's 1937 order parameter theory, and the finite-size rounding of transitions.

Leaves open: if no finite simulation contains a genuine singularity, what exactly is a network detecting when it announces a critical temperature?

verifiedClaims.claim: Josiah Willard Gibbs established the thermodynamic framework for phase equilibria and coexistence in "On the equilibrium of heterogeneous substances," the work that defines chemical potential, the phase rule, surface (interfacial) free energy, and the reversible work of forming a new phase — the thermodynamic ancestor of the nucleation barrier. The full memoir appeared in the Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences (vol. 3, 108-248 in 1876 and 343-524 in 1878); Gibbs published a long abstract in the American Journal of Science in 1878.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Yale College
verifiedClaims.venue: American Journal of Science, ser. 3, vol. 16, no. 96, pp. 441-458 (abstract of the Transactions of the Connecticut Academy memoir, 1876-1878)

verifiedClaims.claim: Paul Ehrenfest proposed classifying phase transitions by the order of the lowest derivative of the thermodynamic potential that is discontinuous: a first-order transition has a discontinuity in the first derivative (hence latent heat and a jump in entropy and volume), a second-order transition has continuous first derivatives but a discontinuous second derivative (specific heat, compressibility, thermal expansion). The paper is "Phasenumwandlungen im ueblichen und erweiterten Sinn, classifiziert nach den entsprechenden Singularitaeten des thermodynamischen Potentiales," Proceedings of the Royal Academy of Sciences at Amsterdam 36, 153-157 (1933), issued simultaneously as Communications from the Kamerlingh Onnes Laboratory, Leiden, Supplement No. 75b. An English translation with historical commentary by Tilman Sauer appeared in 2016. Books must note that Ehrenfest's higher-order categories are now obsolete: continuous transitions generically show power-law divergences, not finite jumps, so modern usage is "first-order" versus "continuous."
verifiedClaims.people: Paul Ehrenfest; Tilman Sauer (translator and commentator)
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Leiden University (Ehrenfest)
verifiedClaims.venue: Proc. Royal Acad. Amsterdam 36, 153-157 (1933), Commun. Kamerlingh Onnes Lab. Leiden Suppl. 75b; translation in European Physical Journal Special Topics (2016), doi:10.1140/epjst/e2016-60344-y

verifiedClaims.claim: Lev Davidovich Landau introduced the order parameter and the expansion of the free energy in powers of it near a continuous transition, deriving mean-field critical exponents (beta = 1/2, gamma = 1, delta = 3, alpha = 0 with a jump in specific heat) and the rule that a continuous transition requires the low-symmetry phase's symmetry group to be a subgroup of the high-symmetry phase's. Originally published in Russian as "K teorii fazovykh perekhodov," Zhurnal Eksperimental'noi i Teoreticheskoi Fiziki 7, 19-32 (1937), with a German version in Physikalische Zeitschrift der Sowjetunion 11, 26 (1937). The standard English text is in Collected Papers of L. D. Landau, edited by D. ter Haar (Pergamon, 1965), pp. 193-216.
verifiedClaims.venue: Zh. Eksp. Teor. Fiz. 7, 19-32 (1937); English translation in Collected Papers of L. D. Landau (Pergamon, 1965), pp. 193-216

verifiedClaims.claim: Ernst Ising solved the one-dimensional version of the model his doctoral supervisor Wilhelm Lenz had proposed and found no phase transition at any nonzero temperature; Ising incorrectly extrapolated this conclusion to higher dimensions. The paper is "Beitrag zur Theorie des Ferromagnetismus," Zeitschrift fuer Physik 31, 253-258 (1925). A book should credit Lenz with the model and Ising with the one-dimensional solution, and should not repeat the myth that Ising proved there is no transition in two dimensions.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Hamburg

verifiedClaims.claim: Rudolf Peierls gave the first argument that the two-dimensional Ising model does order at low temperature, by bounding the entropy versus energy cost of domain-wall contours — the "Peierls argument," still the standard textbook proof that a transition exists. Published as "On Ising's model of ferromagnetism," Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 32, 477-481 (1936).
verifiedClaims.venue: Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 32(3), 477-481

verifiedClaims.claim: Lars Onsager obtained the exact partition function of the two-dimensional square-lattice Ising model in zero field, demonstrating a genuine continuous phase transition with a logarithmically divergent specific heat (alpha = 0, log) and the exact critical temperature given by sinh(2J/kT_c) = 1, i.e. kT_c/J = 2/ln(1 + sqrt(2)) ~ 2.269. This was the first exact demonstration that a microscopic model produces non-mean-field critical behaviour, and it killed the assumption that critical exponents are classical. Published as "Crystal Statistics. I. A Two-Dimensional Model with an Order-Disorder Transition," Physical Review 65, 117-149 (1 February 1944).
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Yale University

verifiedClaims.claim: Chen Ning Yang published the first derivation of the spontaneous magnetization of the two-dimensional Ising model, giving the order-parameter exponent beta = 1/8. Onsager had announced the result in 1948 without publishing a proof, so the exponent should be attributed to Yang's 1952 paper (with Onsager's priority acknowledged), not to the 1944 Onsager paper. Published as "The Spontaneous Magnetization of a Two-Dimensional Ising Model," Physical Review 85, 808-816 (1952).
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton

verifiedClaims.claim: Edward Armand Guggenheim showed that the liquid-gas coexistence curves of eight different substances (neon, argon, krypton, xenon, nitrogen, oxygen, carbon monoxide, methane) collapse onto a single curve when scaled by critical parameters, and that the curve is fitted by an exponent near 1/3 rather than the van der Waals mean-field value 1/2. This is the classic experimental evidence for universality and for non-classical exponents, predating the renormalization group by a quarter century. Published as "The Principle of Corresponding States," Journal of Chemical Physics 13(7), 253-261 (1945).

Benjamin Widom proposed the scaling hypothesis for the equation of state near a critical point — that the singular part of the free energy is a generalized homogeneous function of temperature and field — from which the scaling relations among critical exponents (including alpha + 2*beta + gamma = 2, later called the Rushbrooke relation, and gamma = beta*(delta - 1), the Widom relation) follow. Published as "Equation of State in the Neighborhood of the Critical Point," Journal of Chemical Physics 43(11), 3898-3905 (1965). Scaling here is phenomenological; it is Wilson's renormalization group that later explains why it holds.

Leo Philip Kadanoff introduced the block-spin construction: divide an Ising lattice into cells large compared with the lattice spacing but small compared with the correlation length, replace each cell by a single effective spin, and argue that the coarse-grained system is again an Ising model with rescaled coupling and field. This gave a physical rationale for Widom scaling and is the conceptual seed of the renormalization group. Published as "Scaling laws for Ising models near T_c," Physics Physique Fizika 2, 263-272 (1966) — note the unusual short-lived journal name, often miscited simply as "Physics."
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Illinois, Urbana

verifiedClaims.claim: Kenneth Geddes Wilson turned Kadanoff's block-spin picture into a systematic calculational method by casting coarse-graining as a differential flow in the space of coupling constants, with critical points appearing as fixed points of the flow and critical exponents as eigenvalues of the linearized flow about the fixed point. Universality follows because distinct microscopic Hamiltonians flow to the same fixed point. Published as a pair of companion papers: "Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena. I. Renormalization Group and the Kadanoff Scaling Picture," Physical Review B 4, 3174-3183, and "II. Phase-Space Cell Analysis of Critical Behavior," Physical Review B 4, 3184-3205, both 1971.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: Kenneth G. Wilson and Michael E. Fisher introduced the epsilon expansion, computing critical exponents in d = 4 - epsilon dimensions as a controlled perturbative series about the upper critical dimension four, where mean-field theory becomes exact. Setting epsilon = 1 gives usable three-dimensional exponents. Published as "Critical Exponents in 3.99 Dimensions," Physical Review Letters 28(4), 240-243, issue dated 24 January 1972.
verifiedClaims.people: Kenneth G. Wilson, Michael E. Fisher
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: Michael Ellis Fisher wrote the standard introductory review of the renormalization group approach to critical behaviour, covering the dependence of exponents on dimensionality d, on the number of order-parameter components n, and on the range and anisotropy of interactions — that is, the precise content of a universality class. Published as "The renormalization group in the theory of critical behavior," Reviews of Modern Physics 46, 597-616 (1 October 1974). Note a common citation error: Reviews of Modern Physics 47, 543 (1975) is the erratum, not the article.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 1982 was awarded to Kenneth G. Wilson alone, "for his theory for critical phenomena in connection with phase transitions." Wilson was a professor of physics at Cornell University, where he did the prizewinning work. Michael E. Fisher and Leo P. Kadanoff, whose work was essential to the development, did not share the prize — a point books frequently get wrong; the three were, however, jointly awarded the Wolf Prize in Physics in 1980.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University
verifiedClaims.venue: Nobel Prize in Physics, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

verifiedClaims.claim: Norman David Mermin and Herbert Wagner proved that continuous symmetries cannot be spontaneously broken at any nonzero temperature in one- or two-dimensional systems with sufficiently short-range interactions, ruling out conventional long-range order in the 2D Heisenberg and XY models. This theorem is the obstacle that the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless mechanism circumvents, since BKT order is topological rather than conventional. Published as "Absence of Ferromagnetism or Antiferromagnetism in One- or Two-Dimensional Isotropic Heisenberg Models," Physical Review Letters 17(22), 1133-1136 (1966).

Vadim Lvovich Berezinskii independently identified the destruction of long-range order by topological excitations in two-dimensional systems with continuous symmetry, publishing before Kosterlitz and Thouless. The paper is "Destruction of Long-range Order in One-dimensional and Two-dimensional Systems having a Continuous Symmetry Group. I. Classical Systems," Soviet Physics JETP 32(3), 493 (March 1971); Russian original ZhETF 59(3), 907 (1971). This is why the transition is properly called the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition; Berezinskii died in 1980 and was therefore ineligible for the 2016 Nobel Prize.
verifiedClaims.venue: Soviet Physics JETP 32(3), 493-500 (Russian original: Zhurnal Eksperimental'noi i Teoreticheskoi Fiziki 59(3), 907)

verifiedClaims.claim: John Michael Kosterlitz and David James Thouless defined topological order for two-dimensional systems that have no conventional long-range order, and described a transition driven by the unbinding of vortex-antivortex pairs: below the transition vortices are bound in neutral pairs, above it they are free, destroying superfluid stiffness. The transition is infinite-order in the Ehrenfest sense — the free energy is non-analytic but all derivatives are continuous, and the correlation length diverges exponentially rather than as a power law. Published as "Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems," Journal of Physics C: Solid State Physics 6(7), 1181-1203 (1973). Kosterlitz supplied the renormalization-group treatment the following year in J. Phys. C 7, 1046-1060 (1974).
verifiedClaims.people: John Michael Kosterlitz, David James Thouless
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Birmingham
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Physics C: Solid State Physics 6(7), 1181-1203

verifiedClaims.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2016 was awarded "for theoretical discoveries of topological phase transitions and topological phases of matter," with one half to David J. Thouless (University of Washington, Seattle) and the other half jointly to F. Duncan M. Haldane (Princeton University) and J. Michael Kosterlitz (Brown University). Books must get the split right: it was one-half / one-quarter / one-quarter, not an equal three-way division.
verifiedClaims.people: David J. Thouless, F. Duncan M. Haldane, J. Michael Kosterlitz
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Washington (Thouless); Princeton University (Haldane); Brown University (Kosterlitz)
verifiedClaims.venue: Nobel Prize in Physics, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

verifiedClaims.claim: John A. Hertz formulated the theory of zero-temperature (quantum) critical points by using Hubbard-Stratonovich functional integral transformations to build a quantum generalization of the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson functional in which the order-parameter field depends on imaginary time as well as space. This introduces the dynamical critical exponent z and the effective dimension d + z, so that quantum critical points in three dimensions can sit at or above the upper critical dimension. Published as "Quantum critical phenomena," Physical Review B 14(3), 1165-1184 (1 August 1976). The framework, extended by A. J. Millis in 1993, is standard as "Hertz-Millis theory."
verifiedClaims.affiliation: The James Franck Institute and Department of Physics, University of Chicago

verifiedClaims.claim: Subir Sachdev wrote the standard monograph on quantum phase transitions — transitions at absolute zero driven by a non-thermal control parameter such as pressure, magnetic field, or doping, where quantum rather than thermal fluctuations drive the change, and where the quantum critical point governs a fan-shaped finite-temperature region of anomalous behaviour. The book is Quantum Phase Transitions, Cambridge University Press; first edition 1999 (written while Sachdev was at Yale University), second edition 2011 (Harvard University), ISBN 978-0-521-51468-2. An accessible companion is Sachdev and Bernhard Keimer, "Quantum criticality," Physics Today 64(2), 29-35 (2011), doi:10.1063/1.3554314.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Harvard University (2nd edition); Yale University (1st edition)

verifiedClaims.claim: Simon Ralph Broadbent and John Michael Hammersley founded percolation theory, introducing the distinction between a random "medium" and a deterministic "fluid" and establishing the existence of a sharp critical probability p_c above which an infinite connected cluster appears. Percolation is the canonical purely geometric continuous phase transition, with its own critical exponents and universality classes and no Hamiltonian or temperature. Published as "Percolation processes. I. Crystals and mazes," Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 53(3), 629-641 (July 1957).
verifiedClaims.people: Simon Ralph Broadbent, John Michael Hammersley
verifiedClaims.venue: Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 53(3), 629-641

verifiedClaims.claim: Samuel Frederick Edwards and Philip Warren Anderson introduced the first theory of spin glasses, proposing that in dilute magnetic alloys the RKKY interaction oscillates in sign with distance so that there is no net ferro- or antiferromagnetic order, yet below a freezing temperature the spins lock into definite random directions. Their order parameter q — the time-averaged local magnetization squared, averaged over sites — is the Edwards-Anderson order parameter, and it explains the cusp observed experimentally in the susceptibility. Published as "Theory of spin glasses," Journal of Physics F: Metal Physics 5(5), 965-974 (May 1975); a second part appeared in J. Phys. F 6, 1927 (1976).
verifiedClaims.people: Samuel Frederick Edwards, Philip Warren Anderson
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge
verifiedClaims.venue: Journal of Physics F: Metal Physics 5(5), 965-974

verifiedClaims.claim: David Sherrington and Scott Kirkpatrick introduced the infinite-range (mean-field) spin glass: an Ising model in which every pair of spins is coupled by an independent Gaussian random interaction. Solving it by the replica trick with a replica-symmetric ansatz, they found both spin-glass and ferromagnetic phases — but the solution gives a negative entropy at zero temperature, an unphysical result that signalled the breakdown of replica symmetry and set the problem Parisi later solved. Published as "Solvable Model of a Spin-Glass," Physical Review Letters 35(26), 1792-1796 (1975).

Giorgio Parisi showed that the mean-field spin glass requires an infinite number of order parameters — a full function q(x) on the interval [0,1] rather than a single number — obtained by breaking the permutation symmetry among replicas in a nested, hierarchical (ultrametric) way. This is replica symmetry breaking, and it describes a rugged free-energy landscape with many pure states organized in a hierarchy. Published as "Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses," Physical Review Letters 43(23), 1754-1756 (received 22 June 1979, published 3 December 1979), with the explicit scheme in "A sequence of approximated solutions to the S-K model for spin glasses," Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and General 13(4), L115-L121 (1980). The solution's correctness was proved rigorously by Michel Talagrand in 2006, building on Francesco Guerra's 2003 interpolation bound.
verifiedClaims.venue: Physical Review Letters 43(23), 1754-1756; Journal of Physics A 13(4), L115-L121

verifiedClaims.claim: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2021 was awarded "for groundbreaking contributions to our understanding of complex systems," divided with one half jointly to Syukuro Manabe and Klaus Hasselmann for physical modelling of Earth's climate, and the other half to Giorgio Parisi (Sapienza University of Rome) "for the discovery of the interplay of disorder and fluctuations in physical systems from atomic to planetary scales." Parisi's citation dates the key discovery to around 1980. Books should not describe this as a prize shared equally three ways, nor as a prize for spin glasses alone.
verifiedClaims.people: Giorgio Parisi, Syukuro Manabe, Klaus Hasselmann
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Sapienza University of Rome (Parisi)
verifiedClaims.venue: Nobel Prize in Physics, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

verifiedClaims.claim: Philip Warren Anderson argued that the reductionist hypothesis does not imply a constructionist one: at each level of complexity entirely new properties appear, and the science of one level is not simply applied science of the level below. Broken symmetry — exactly the phenomenon that defines a phase transition — is his central example of how new organizing principles emerge at larger scales. Published as "More Is Different: Broken symmetry and the nature of the hierarchical structure of science," Science 177(4047), 393-396, 4 August 1972. This is the canonical citation for emergence in phase-transition writing.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey

verifiedClaims.claim: Max Volmer and Alfred Weber laid the foundation of classical nucleation theory, treating the formation of a nucleus in a supersaturated phase as a competition between a favourable bulk free-energy term proportional to volume and an unfavourable interfacial term proportional to surface area, producing a free-energy barrier at a critical nucleus size and a nucleation rate exponential in that barrier. Published as "Keimbildung in uebersaettigten Gebilden," Zeitschrift fuer Physikalische Chemie 119U(1), 277-301 (1926).

Richard Becker and Werner Doering gave the kinetic formulation of classical nucleation theory, treating nucleation as a birth-and-death process in cluster size space and deriving the steady-state nucleation rate including the Zeldovich non-equilibrium correction factor. The resulting Becker-Doering equations remain the standard kinetic model of nucleation. Published as "Kinetische Behandlung der Keimbildung in uebersaettigten Daempfen," Annalen der Physik 416(8), 719-752 (1935).

David Turnbull and John Chipman Fisher adapted classical nucleation theory to condensed systems, supplying the rate expression with an activation term for the transport of atoms across the nucleus-matrix interface — the form used for crystallization from melts and solutions, and the basis for Turnbull's later experiments showing that liquid metals can be supercooled to roughly 0.8 of their melting temperature before nucleating. Published as "Rate of Nucleation in Condensed Systems," Journal of Chemical Physics 17(1), 71-73 (1949).

Wilhelm Ostwald formulated the rule of stages (Ostwald's Stufenregel): a supersaturated or supercooled system does not necessarily transform directly into the thermodynamically most stable phase, but tends first to form the least stable phase whose free energy is nearest to that of the parent phase, then transforms stepwise toward stability. This is a kinetic, not a thermodynamic, principle, and it underlies polymorph selection in crystallization. Published as "Studien ueber die Bildung und Umwandlung fester Koerper. 1. Abhandlung: Uebersaettigung und Ueberkaltung," Zeitschrift fuer Physikalische Chemie 22U(1), 289-330 (1897).
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Leipzig

verifiedClaims.claim: John Werner Cahn and John Edward Hilliard introduced the square-gradient free-energy functional for a system of nonuniform composition, F = N_V * integral over V of [f_0(c) + kappa*(grad c)^2] dV, where f_0 is the homogeneous free energy per molecule and kappa the gradient-energy coefficient. This is the basis of all diffuse-interface and phase-field modelling of transitions. Published as "Free Energy of a Nonuniform System. I. Interfacial Free Energy," Journal of Chemical Physics 28(2), 258-267 (1958). Part III of the series, "Nucleation in a Two-Component Incompressible Fluid," J. Chem. Phys. 31(3), 688-699 (1959), doi:10.1063/1.1730447, derives the critical nucleus as a saddle point of this functional and shows the classical sharp-interface nucleus fails near the spinodal.
verifiedClaims.people: John Werner Cahn, John Edward Hilliard
verifiedClaims.affiliation: General Electric Research Laboratory, Schenectady, New York

verifiedClaims.claim: John Werner Cahn established the theory of spinodal decomposition: inside the spinodal region, where the second derivative of free energy with respect to composition is negative, a homogeneous solution is unstable to infinitesimal composition fluctuations, so phase separation proceeds by spontaneous continuous amplification of long-wavelength fluctuations with no nucleation barrier and no critical nucleus — in sharp contrast to nucleation and growth in the metastable region between the binodal and the spinodal. Cahn derived the fastest-growing wavelength that sets the characteristic microstructural scale, and showed that elastic energy from composition-dependent molar volume shifts the true limit of metastability away from the chemical spinodal. Published as "On spinodal decomposition," Acta Metallurgica 9(9), 795-801 (1961); the cubic-crystal extension is Acta Metallurgica 10(3), 179-183 (1962).
verifiedClaims.affiliation: General Electric Research Laboratory, Schenectady, New York

verifiedClaims.claim: Original memoir in which Clapeyron reformulated Carnot's argument analytically and derived the relation between the latent heat of a phase change and the slope of the coexistence curve — the ancestor of dp/dT = L/(T*Delta V). Published in the Journal de l'Ecole Royale Polytechnique, vingt-troisieme cahier, Tome XIV. No DOI exists; a facsimile is held by the Bibliotheque nationale de France (Gallica).
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Ecole des Ponts et Chaussees / Ecole Polytechnique, Paris
verifiedClaims.venue: Memoire sur la puissance motrice de la chaleur, Journal de l'Ecole Royale Polytechnique, Tome XIV (23e cahier), pp. 153-190

verifiedClaims.claim: Clausius's founding paper of thermodynamics, in two parts, where the Carnot-Clapeyron relation is recast on the basis of the two laws and put into the modern form now called the Clausius-Clapeyron relation; Part II carries DOI 10.1002/andp.18501550403 (Ann. Phys. 155(4), 500-524). Crossref confirms both parts. Note the volume is Annalen der Physik 155 (also catalogued as vol. 79 of the old series).
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Royal Artillery and Engineering School, Berlin
verifiedClaims.venue: Annalen der Physik 155(3), 368-397 (Part I) and 155(4), 500-524 (Part II)

verifiedClaims.claim: Modern, citable, DOI-bearing pedagogical treatment of the Clausius-Clapeyron equation dp/dT = L/(T*Delta V), including the standard approximations (ideal-gas vapour, Delta V approximately equal to V_gas) and where they break down against measured saturation vapour pressure. Useful when the book needs a present-day reference rather than the 1850 original.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: National Technical University of Athens

verifiedClaims.claim: Standard graduate textbook source for the Clausius-Clapeyron relation and first-order coexistence within a statistical-mechanics course; the companion volume is Statistical Physics of Fields (DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511815881), which carries the Ginzburg criterion and the upper critical dimension. Cambridge assigns a DOI to the electronic edition, so this is citable with a DOI unlike Callen or Landau-Lifshitz.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
verifiedClaims.venue: Statistical Physics of Particles, Cambridge University Press (print ISBN 9780521873420)

verifiedClaims.claim: Part I of the Yang-Lee theory. Establishes that for a finite system the grand partition function is a polynomial in the fugacity z with no zeros on the positive real axis, hence the free energy is analytic and there is no singularity; that in the thermodynamic limit the zeros may migrate onto and pinch the positive real z axis; and that the free energy is analytic throughout any region of the complex z plane containing no zeros, so a phase transition occurs exactly at a pinch point. AUTHOR ORDER: Yang first, Lee second. Crossref confirms 'C. N. Yang, T. D. Lee'.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton; Columbia University

verifiedClaims.claim: Part II of the Yang-Lee theory. Introduces the lattice gas and proves its exact equivalence to the Ising model in a magnetic field, and proves the Lee-Yang circle theorem: for a ferromagnetic Ising system all zeros of the partition function in the complex fugacity (equivalently complex magnetic-field) plane lie on the unit circle |z| = 1, i.e. at purely imaginary values of the field. AUTHOR ORDER IS REVERSED FROM PART I: Lee first, Yang second. Crossref confirms 'T. D. Lee, C. N. Yang'.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Columbia University; Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton

verifiedClaims.claim: The standard modern generalisation of the Lee-Yang circle theorem, extending it well beyond the Ising case to one-component and multicomponent ferromagnets with quite general single-spin measures. This is the reference to cite when the book claims the circle theorem is not a peculiarity of the Ising model.
verifiedClaims.people: Elliott H. Lieb, Alan D. Sokal
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Princeton University; New York University (at time of publication)

verifiedClaims.claim: The best single review of the whole partition-function-zeros programme: Yang-Lee zeros in complex fugacity, Fisher zeros in complex temperature, the density of zeros and how its pinching angle encodes the order of the transition, and extensions to nonequilibrium steady states. Its Section 12 is where Fisher zeros are defined and Fisher's 1965 Boulder lectures are credited. Preprint arXiv:cond-mat/0510278 (2005); journal version same year.
verifiedClaims.people: Ioana Bena, Michel Droz, Adam Lipowski
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Geneva; Adam Mickiewicz University, Poznan
verifiedClaims.venue: International Journal of Modern Physics B 19, 4269-4329

verifiedClaims.claim: Fisher's Boulder lecture notes, the origin of what is now universally called the Fisher zeros: the proposal to study phase transitions via the zeros of the CANONICAL partition function in the plane of complex TEMPERATURE, complementing Yang and Lee's zeros in complex fugacity. In a finite system these zeros lie off the positive real temperature axis; they close in on it in the thermodynamic limit. There is no DOI and no journal version. Cite as: M. E. Fisher, 'The Nature of Critical Points', in Lectures in Theoretical Physics, Vol. 7c: Statistical Physics, Weak Interactions, Field Theory, ed. W. E. Brittin (University of Colorado Press, Boulder, 1965), pp. 1-159. Lectures were delivered at the 1964 Boulder Summer Institute for Theoretical Physics; the volume appeared in 1965.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: The Rockefeller Institute, New York (as printed on the lectures)
verifiedClaims.venue: Lectures in Theoretical Physics, Vol. 7c, ed. W. E. Brittin, University of Colorado Press, Boulder, pp. 1-159

verifiedClaims.claim: Identifies the Yang-Lee edge — the endpoint of the arc of zeros on the unit circle above T_c — as a genuine critical point in its own right, with its own exponent sigma, and shows it is governed by a non-unitary i*phi-cubed field theory with upper critical dimension 6. The result that turns 'zeros on a circle' from a curiosity into a universality class.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: Direct experimental observation of Lee-Yang zeros, obtained by measuring the quantum coherence of a probe spin coupled to an Ising-type bath in an NMR system, which encodes the partition function at complex magnetic field. Cite this if the book wants to answer the objection that complex-field zeros are a purely formal device.
verifiedClaims.people: Xinhua Peng, Hui Zhou, Bo-Bo Wei, Jiangyu Cui, Jiangfeng Du, Ren-Bao Liu
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei; Chinese University of Hong Kong

verifiedClaims.claim: The first statement of the finite-size scaling idea: at a critical point the singular behaviour of a bounded system is rounded and shifted, and both the shift and the rounding are controlled by the ratio of the correlation length to the system size. The precursor to the 1972 Fisher-Barber paper.
verifiedClaims.people: Michael E. Fisher, Arthur E. Ferdinand
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: Exact solution for the specific heat of a FINITE two-dimensional Ising lattice (n by m, torus and other boundary conditions). This is the concrete demonstration that a finite Ising system has no singularity at all — the specific heat is a smooth, bounded, analytic function of temperature whose peak grows only as log(L) and sits at a shifted pseudo-critical temperature. The exact worked example a graduate reader can check against their own simulation.
verifiedClaims.people: Arthur E. Ferdinand, Michael E. Fisher
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: THE canonical finite-size scaling citation. States the scaling theory with distinct exponents lambda for the critical-point shift and theta = 1/nu for the rounding, so that the width of the rounded region scales as L^(-1/nu) and the peak height as a power of L; verified against exact results for d-dimensional spherical models and ideal Bose fluids with various boundary conditions, and checked against Ising data and helium-film experiments. This is the standard citable statement that a finite system has no true singularity and that the rounding scales as a power of the system size. The book-length companion statement is M. N. Barber, 'Finite-size scaling', in Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena, Vol. 8, ed. C. Domb and J. L. Lebowitz (Academic Press, London, 1983), pp. 145-266 — no DOI located for that chapter.
verifiedClaims.people: Michael E. Fisher, Michael N. Barber
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: Introduces the fourth-order cumulant of the order-parameter block distribution — the Binder cumulant — whose curves for different L cross at T_c, giving the workhorse numerical method for locating a critical point from finite lattices without knowing the exponents in advance. Directly usable in an Ising-simulation chapter.

verifiedClaims.claim: Establishes that finite-size scaling functions and their amplitudes are themselves universal, given a fixed shape, boundary conditions and aspect ratio — the result that licenses quantitative collapse of data from different lattice sizes onto one curve. NOTE: Crossref misprints the first author as 'Valdimir Privman'; the correct spelling is Vladimir Privman.

verifiedClaims.claim: Priority note for the Ginzburg criterion. Levanyuk, as sole author and a year before Ginzburg, gave the fluctuation-magnitude estimate that bounds the validity of Landau theory near a second-order transition, in the context of critical opalescence and light scattering. Because of this the criterion is more accurately called the Levanyuk-Ginzburg criterion. English translation Sov. Phys. JETP 9(3), 571 (September 1959); Russian original ZhETF 36(3), 810 (1959); received 8 July 1958. No DOI; the JETP archive hosts the scan at the URL given.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: USSR Academy of Sciences

verifiedClaims.claim: The Ginzburg criterion. States the self-consistency condition for mean-field (Landau) theory: the theory is valid only where fluctuations of the order parameter within a correlation volume are small compared with the order parameter itself. This bounds the reduced temperature outside which mean-field exponents hold and inside which they must fail, with the width of the critical (Ginzburg) region scaling as the inverse sixth power of the interaction range — which is why the region is unobservably narrow in conventional superconductors and ferroelectrics but wide in short-range magnets. Russian original: Fiz. Tverd. Tela 2, 2031 (1960). English translation: 'Some remarks on phase transitions of the second kind and the microscopic theory of ferroelectric materials', Sov. Phys. Solid State 2(9), 1824-1834; indexes disagree on whether the translation is dated 1960 or 1961. No DOI.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: P. N. Lebedev Physical Institute, Moscow
verifiedClaims.venue: Fizika Tverdogo Tela 2, 2031 (1960) [Soviet Physics Solid State 2(9), 1824-1834]

verifiedClaims.claim: The standard English-language pedagogical statement of the Ginzburg criterion, with the criterion derived explicitly and used to define the marginal (upper critical) dimensionality at which mean-field theory becomes self-consistent — namely d = 4 for short-range systems with a scalar order parameter. The most quotable single source for 'when is mean-field theory allowed to be right'.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Risoe National Laboratory, Denmark; Massachusetts Institute of Technology

verifiedClaims.claim: The epsilon expansion. Computes critical exponents as a systematic series in epsilon = 4 - d, i.e. by perturbing around the upper critical dimension of the Ising universality class. The title itself ('Critical Exponents in 3.99 Dimensions') is the cleanest possible signal that d = 4 is the dimension where mean-field behaviour turns on.
verifiedClaims.people: Kenneth G. Wilson, Michael E. Fisher
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Cornell University

verifiedClaims.claim: Rigorous proof that for d > 4 the continuum limit of the phi-fourth field theory is trivial (free/Gaussian) and that Ising models in more than four dimensions exhibit mean-field critical behaviour. This is the theorem behind the statement 'the upper critical dimension of the Ising universality class is 4'. The independent contemporaneous proof is J. Froehlich, Nuclear Physics B 200(2), 281-296 (1982), DOI 10.1016/0550-3213(82)90088-8.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Princeton University

verifiedClaims.claim: Closes the marginal case left open for forty years: proves that in exactly d = 4 the scaling limit of the critical Ising and lambda-phi-fourth models is also Gaussian, though the approach is only logarithmically slow. This is the precise sense in which d = 4 is the upper critical dimension rather than merely a boundary. Preprint arXiv:1912.07973 (2019); journal publication 2021.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Princeton University; IHES and University of Geneva

verifiedClaims.claim: THE CORE SUPERVISED PROTOCOL. Fully connected feed-forward net implemented in TensorFlow: input layer = raw Monte Carlo spin configuration (sigma_i = +/-1, N = L^2 values, no preprocessing), one hidden layer of 100 sigmoid neurons, and a two-unit output layer; cross-entropy cost with an L2 regularization term; trained with Adam. Training data: Monte Carlo configurations over a broad range of temperatures above and below T_c on the square-lattice ferromagnetic Ising model H = -J sum_<ij> sigma_i^z sigma_j^z, J = 1. LABELS ARE BINARY AND SUPERVISED BY THE KNOWN T_c: each configuration is tagged 'low-temperature' or 'high-temperature' according to whether its sampling temperature lies below or above the Onsager value T_c/J = 2/ln(1+sqrt2). The network correctly classifies 94% of an uncorrelated test set at N = L^2 = 10^2, rising to 99% at L = 40. Identical success with antiferromagnetic couplings H = +J sum sigma_i sigma_j, i.e. for an order parameter with ordering wavevector q = (pi/a, pi/a). The paper does NOT claim to discover T_c on the training lattice.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo (Carrasquilla); Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo and Perimeter Institute (Melko)
verifiedClaims.year: 2017 journal; arXiv v1 5 May 2016; received 27 June 2016, accepted 11 January 2017, published online 13 February 2017, issue date May 2017

verifiedClaims.claim: HOW T_c IS EXTRACTED, AND THE ONE-HALF CROSSING. Carrasquilla and Melko extract a critical temperature not on the lattice they trained on but on an unseen one: the square-lattice-trained network is fed Monte Carlo configurations of the TRIANGULAR-lattice ferromagnetic Ising model (L = 30), with no information about the Hamiltonian, the lattice structure, or even the locality of interactions. The two output neurons are averaged over the test set at each temperature and plotted against T; T_c is estimated from their crossing point, giving T_c/J = 3.63581 against the exact 4/ln3 = 3.640957 (arXiv v1 value, single size). Because the two softmax outputs are complementary and sum to one, the crossing is precisely the point where each output equals 0.5 - this is the origin of the 'output crosses one-half' criterion; the arXiv text says 'crossing point of the low- and high-temperature outputs' rather than writing 0.5 explicitly. The analytically constructed three-perceptron toy network, given the same task with no knowledge of either critical temperature, returns T_c/J = 3.63403, under 1% from the exact value.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo

verifiedClaims.claim: FINITE-SIZE SCALING IN THE PUBLISHED VERSION (NOT IN arXiv v1). The Nature Physics version adds a finite-size-scaling analysis absent from the arXiv preprint: system sizes up to L = 60, with the averaged output F^T for the ferromagnetic class shown to collapse when plotted against the scaling variable t*L^(1/nu), t the reduced temperature. The collapse yields T_c = 2.266 +/- 0.002 and nu = 1.0 +/- 0.2, consistent with the exact 2/ln(1+sqrt2) = 2.269 and the exact 2D Ising nu = 1; the triangular-lattice estimate quoted from the same 100-unit network is T_c = 3.65(1). USE WITH CARE: I could not read the paywalled published text directly. These numbers are quoted verbatim by two independent later papers that had the published version in hand - Chertenkov, Burovski & Shchur, PRE 108, L032102 (2023), which states the L <= 60 data collapse and the values 2.266 +/- 0.002 and nu = 1.0 +/- 0.2, and Kim & Kim, PRE 98, 022138 (2018), which quotes 'T_c = 2.266(2) with nu = 1.0(2)' and 'T_c = 3.65(1)' as the 100-unit network results of Carrasquilla2017.
verifiedClaims.people: Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko (values as reported by Vladislav Chertenkov, Evgeni Burovski, Lev Shchur; and by Dongkyu Kim, Dong-Hee Kim)
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Perimeter Institute / University of Waterloo
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Physics 13, 431-434 (2017); confirmed in Phys. Rev. E 108, L032102 (2023) and Phys. Rev. E 98, 022138 (2018)

verifiedClaims.claim: WHAT THE ISING NETWORK IS READING, IN THE ORIGINAL PAPER ITSELF. Carrasquilla and Melko construct an analytic toy replacement for the hidden layer: three Heaviside perceptrons with weight matrix W = (1/(N(1+eps))) * [[1..1],[-1..-1],[1..1]] and bias b = (eps/(1+eps))*(-1,-1,1)^T, so that Wx + b = (1/(1+eps)) * (m(x)-eps, -m(x)-eps, m(x)+eps) where m(x) = (1/N) sum_i sigma_i is exactly the magnetization; eps in (0,1) is a magnetization threshold. Two perceptrons fire on polarized states, the third on 'polarized-up or unpolarized'. They then train a real 3-sigmoid network numerically and show that during training the components of W_t x + b_t become approximately linear functions of m(x), concluding 'These results clearly support our claim about the neural network's ability to encode and learn the magnetization in the hidden layer.' Their own summary sentence: neural networks 'encode information about conventional ordered phases by learning the order parameter of the phase'. A t-SNE embedding of the training set shows two low-T (up/down) lobes and one high-T region separated by a hyperplane.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Physics 13, 431-434 (2017), supplementary material (Appendices A-B of arXiv:1605.01735)

verifiedClaims.claim: THE COULOMB PHASE TEST. Two-dimensional square ice, H = J sum_v Q_v^2 with vertex charge Q_v = sum_{i in v} sigma_i^z and Ising spins on the bonds. The two classes are T = 0 ground states (an extensively degenerate Coulomb phase, power-law spin-spin correlations, no bulk magnetization or any local order parameter) versus high-temperature states (exponentially decaying correlations). Trained on raw configurations with the same standard fully connected 100-hidden-unit network, at N = 2 x 16 x 16 spins it separates the two classes with 99% accuracy, with no information about the underlying lattice. The authors' reading: 'the learning capabilities of neural networks go beyond the simple ability to encode order parameters, extending to the detection of subtle differences in higher-order correlation functions.' This is the surprise - a plain shallow classifier separating states that differ only in the functional form of their correlations.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo

verifiedClaims.claim: THE TORIC-CODE / ISING GAUGE THEORY TEST, AND THE NEGATIVE RESULT. Two-dimensional Ising lattice gauge theory H = -J sum_p prod_{i in p} sigma_i^z, spins on the bonds of a square lattice, ground-state manifold the same as the toric code, exponentially decaying spin-spin correlations. The standard fully connected network FAILS: it cannot exceed 50% accuracy, 'equivalent to simply guessing'. A convolutional network succeeds: 64 filters of size 2x2 convolved on each of the two sublattices, unit stride, no padding, periodic boundary conditions, ReLU, then a 64-unit fully connected ReLU layer with dropout, then a two-output softmax; trained on configurations at T = 0 and T = infinity it reaches 100% accuracy on a 1x10^4-configuration test set. The surprise is what the supplement then shows: (i) flipping one spin every m = 2 (m = 8) plaquettes preserves the topological order but violates local constraints, and accuracy collapses to 50% (55%); (ii) cutting ground states into 4 pieces and restitching pieces from different states destroys the extended closed-loop structure and the topological degeneracy while preserving local constraints almost everywhere - and the CNN still classifies these as ground states with high confidence. Conclusion: 'local constraints are the only features that the CNN relies on'. An analytic toy CNN with 16 2x2 filters per sublattice that literally enumerates the 8 satisfied and 8 unsatisfied plaquette configurations also reaches 100%. So the network is not detecting topological order; it is detecting the Hamiltonian's local energetic constraints.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics; University of Waterloo
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Physics 13, 431-434 (2017), main text and Appendix C

verifiedClaims.claim: LEARNING BY CONFUSION - THE EXACT SCHEME. Data lie in a parameter range (a,b) containing an unknown critical point c. Propose a trial critical point c', label everything below c' as 0 and everything above as 1, train a fresh network N_{c'} on that deliberately-part-wrong labelling, then evaluate its total performance P(c') on the entire data set. Sweeping c' from a to b produces the universal W-SHAPE: P = 1 at c' = a and c' = b (the net assigns one label to everything and is right by construction), P = 1 again at c' = c (the correct labelling), and two minima in between where the net learns the majority label and scores P(c') = 1 - min(c-c', c'-a)/(c-a) for a < c' < c. The middle peak always sits at the correct c; asymmetric placement of c distorts the depths of the two minima but not the peak position. CONTROL: trained on unstructured random data against a fictitious tuning parameter the middle peak disappears and the W becomes a V, so the peak is evidence of real structure. Systems: (1) Kitaev chain, input = the largest 10 entanglement-spectrum eigenvalues for L = 20 with L_A = L_B = 10, transition recovered at mu = -2t; (2) two-dimensional classical Ising, network with L^2 input and L^2 hidden neurons and 2 outputs trained on L x L configurations - the peak deviates from T_c for L = 10 by finite-size effects and sits exactly at k_B T_c ~ 2.27 J for L = 20; (3) many-body localization in a random-field Heisenberg chain, L = 12, 64 entanglement-spectrum levels, 10^5 disorder realizations per field strength, giving h_c ~ 3J. A separate 'blanking' test shows a supervised net trained with a window of width up to w = 3t blanked out around the transition still locates it.
verifiedClaims.people: Evert P. L. van Nieuwenburg; Ye-Hua Liu; Sebastian D. Huber
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zurich

verifiedClaims.claim: UNSUPERVISED BASELINE: PCA FINDS THE MAGNETIZATION. Wang collects 100 uncorrelated Wolff-sampled square-lattice Ising configurations at each of T/J = 1.6, 1.7, ..., 2.9 into an M x N matrix X with M = 1400, and solves X^T X w_l = lambda_l w_l. Exactly ONE dominant explained-variance ratio appears, and the weight vector of the first principal component is flat across all lattice sites - i.e. the first principal component IS the uniform magnetization (1/N) sum_i sigma_i. Projecting onto the first two components separates the samples into three clusters (two ordered, one paramagnetic) that sharpen as N goes 20^2, 40^2, 80^2. For the conserved-order-parameter Ising model (same Hamiltonian, sum_i sigma_i identically zero, so magnetization is useless) there are FOUR leading components with weights cos(theta_i), cos(phi_i), sin(theta_i), sin(phi_i), and the nonlinear combination sum_{l=1..4} y_l^2 is proportional to a structure factor S detecting domain-wall orientational order - a quantity Wang states was unknown to him before the learner found it. He explicitly flags the limitation: PCA is linear, so topological order, duality, Wilson loops and string order remain out of reach.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Institute of Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing

verifiedClaims.claim: THE CRITICAL EXAMINATION - PRECISELY WHAT FAILED AND WHERE. Hu, Singh and Scalettar apply PCA (and an autoencoder) to the square-lattice Ising ferromagnet, triangular-lattice Ising antiferromagnet, Blume-Capel model, a biquadratic-exchange spin-one Ising (BSI) model, and the 2D XY model. SUCCESSES: PCA locates transition temperatures with reasonable accuracy; strong first-order transitions are distinguishable from second-order ones by the evolution of the principal-component distribution; a crossover is distinguishable from a true transition; principal components map onto Fourier modes and order parameters and their size dependence yields critical exponents; in the frustrated triangular antiferromagnet the components point to incipient orders. FAILURES, MODEL BY MODEL: (a) BSI model - feeding raw {S_i} produces NO dominant principal component and a complete mixture of all temperatures in the projection, because the order lives in the checkerboard arrangement of S_i^2 (the 'charge') while PCA averages the S_i = +/-1 variables to zero; feeding {S_i^2} restores a dominant component. (b) 2D XY model - feeding raw local vorticity (plaquette winding number +1, 0, -1) again gives no dominant component, because equal numbers of vortices and antivortices cancel; feeding ABSOLUTE vorticity (1 if a vortex or antivortex is present, 0 otherwise) recovers a dominant component, but the signal 'appears more like a crossover than a true phase transition', and the authors write that seeing the vortex-antivortex unbinding transition 'may be difficult in PCA or any machine learning technique'. They also establish that the BSI model has no phase transition and a macroscopic ground-state degeneracy. Overall lesson: the answer depends on which representation (bare spins vs bond, triangle, plaquette or vorticity variables) is fed in, and one is not recoverable from the other.
verifiedClaims.people: Wenjian Hu; Rajiv R. P. Singh; Richard T. Scalettar
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics (and Department of Computer Science), University of California, Davis

verifiedClaims.claim: PCA TO VARIATIONAL AUTOENCODERS ON THE ISING MODEL. Wetzel samples the 2D Ising model on L = 28 (N = 784) with periodic boundaries, 50,000 configurations for the ferromagnet over T in [0,5] (10,000 for the antiferromagnet), and the 3D XY model on L = 14 (N = 2744). He compares four unsupervised methods with a single latent variable each: PCA, kernel PCA, a plain autoencoder, and a variational autoencoder (one fully connected 256-neuron hidden layer in encoder and in decoder). Result: the latent parameter of all four correlates cleanly with the magnetization, i.e. the learned latent variable IS the known order parameter; PCA is the most accurate, the VAE close behind, the plain autoencoder inaccurate (which is his stated motivation for the variational version). Separately he shows the mean-squared-error reconstruction loss, averaged at fixed temperature, changes character at T_c and proposes it as a 'universal identifier for phase transitions' requiring no order parameter. The latent representations cluster, allowing phases to be identified without prior knowledge of their existence or of the Hamiltonian.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Institut fuer Theoretische Physik, Universitaet Heidelberg

verifiedClaims.claim: THE SHARPEST PUBLISHED ANSWER TO 'MAGNETIZATION OR ENERGY?'. Wetzel and Scherzer build a 'correlation probing neural network': a fully convolutional localization subnetwork whose output neurons have a FIXED receptive field, an averaging layer that destroys all spatial information, and a fully connected prediction subnetwork. Restricting the receptive field restricts which spin correlations the decision function can possibly contain. Trained on 2D Ising configurations sampled below T = 1.6 and above T = 2.9 (L = 28): (i) at receptive field 1x1 the decision function is provably D(S) = F((1/N) sum_i sigma_i), since sigma_i^2 = 1 kills all higher Taylor terms; its latent prediction xi is PERFECTLY correlated with |m| and NOT correlated with the average product of neighbouring spins, and its P = 0.5 crossing gives only T = 2.5 +/- 0.5. (ii) At receptive field 1x2 the latent prediction is perfectly correlated with the average nearest-neighbour product - the expected energy per site - and NOT with the norm of the average spin; crossing gives T = 2.25 +/- 0.25, and the loss drops sharply relative to 1x1. (iii) Enlarging the receptive field from 1x2 all the way to the full 28x28 (equivalent to an unrestricted CNN) produces NO further drop in training or validation loss. Conclusion stated in the abstract: 'the neural network predicts the phase by the magnetization and the expected energy per spin' - and nothing beyond nearest-neighbour correlations is used. The same pipeline applied to SU(2) lattice gauge theory reconstructs the Polyakov loop as the decision function.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Institut fuer Theoretische Physik, Universitaet Heidelberg

verifiedClaims.claim: THE MAGNETIZATION STORY DEPENDS ON THE MONTE CARLO UPDATE. Suchsland and Wessel note that the Carrasquilla-Melko low-temperature training set was generated with the Wolff cluster algorithm, which yields strongly polarized low-T configurations containing NO extended domain walls (EDW) - and that this is what makes the 'network learns the magnetization' picture hold. Once a significant fraction of EDW configurations is included in the low-T set (as happens naturally with local spin updates), a fully connected network's hidden-layer activations show 'no clear overall relation' to the magnetization except at large |m|, and instead exhibit 'traces of a linear relation between the activations and the configurational energy'; the network 'performs the classification task based on a combined representation of the energy and the magnetization'. They further show a shallow CNN with N_k = 8 fixed 2x2 ReLU filters (a layout modelled on Carrasquilla-Melko) handles EDW configurations efficiently precisely because its filters can pick up local contributions to BOTH the magnetization and the local configurational energy. They also combine learning-by-confusion with a simple threshold-value classifier as a diagnostic for what a network has learned, and contrast bare-spin against vortex-preprocessed inputs for the 2D XY model.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Institut fuer Theoretische Festkoerperphysik, JARA-FIT and JARA-HPC, RWTH Aachen University

verifiedClaims.claim: MAGNETIZATION IN FULLY CONNECTED LAYERS, INTERNAL ENERGY IN CONVOLUTIONAL ONES. Kashiwa, Kikuchi and Tomiya train networks on 2D Ising and Potts configurations labelled by TEMPERATURE (20 target couplings K = 0.05, 0.10, ..., 1.0 at L = 16), never telling the network which phase a configuration is in, and then dissect the trained weights. For a fully connected network (hidden layer reduced from 80 to 5 and then 3 units) the first-layer outputs x_a = w_ai sigma_i + b_a are cleanly correlated with the magnetization per site of the input configuration, and the second-layer weights change structure at the exact critical coupling K_c = 0.4407. For a convolutional network (filters of size 2,2,4 with 64, 32, 3 channels, giving N_h = 3 hidden units) the picture flips: 'We clearly see the transition in what the neural network has learned. The first-layer outputs are now proportional to the internal energy rather than the magnetization of input configurations.' Their explanation: the internal energy varies far more strongly with temperature than |m| away from T_c, so a network optimizing temperature prediction prefers it - which is also why the CNN attains roughly twice the temperature-prediction accuracy of the fully connected net.
verifiedClaims.people: Kouji Kashiwa; Yuta Kikuchi; Akio Tomiya
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Fukuoka Institute of Technology (Kashiwa); RIKEN BNL Research Center, Brookhaven National Laboratory (Kikuchi, Tomiya)

verifiedClaims.claim: THE SMALLEST NETWORK, AND THE EXPLICIT ONE-HALF DEFINITION. Kim and Kim reduce the hidden layer to TWO neurons with weights fixed by Z_2 symmetry so that the hidden arguments are +/-(y - mu) with y = (1/N) sum_i s_i, and the output is q = [1 + tanh(Lambda z)]/2 with only two trainable parameters Lambda and mu. They define the pseudotransition temperature explicitly by <q>_{T*} = 1/2, the averaged output crossing one half. Solving the training problem analytically they find that the learned parameters encode the SCALING DIMENSION of the order parameter: Lambda_L ~ L^{2 Delta_sigma} and mu_L - ln3 ~ L^{-2 Delta_sigma} with Delta_sigma = beta/nu. Numerically, extrapolating T*_L for the square lattice gives T*_infinity = 2.267(1) with nu = 0.94(2) - matching the 100-unit network's 2.266(2) with nu = 1.0(2); the same square-lattice-trained network gives T_c ~ 3.637 on the triangular lattice (vs 3.65(1) from the 100-unit net) and a clean collapse at the exact 4/ln3 with nu = 1. This is the mechanism behind the transferability across lattices: same universality class, same scaling dimension. Applied instead to the 3D Ising model, the 2D-trained network's output curves develop NO crossing at all and converge to a wrong T*_infinity ~ 4.4695; using the correct 3D Delta_sigma = 0.51815 and nu = 0.63 recovers T_c = 4.51152(1).
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics and Photon Science, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST), Gwangju, Korea

verifiedClaims.claim: THE ONE-HALF CRITERION STATED IN WORDS, AND FITTING PROCEDURE. The companion paper to Carrasquilla-Melko, by the same group plus Ch'ng and Khatami, is the place where the criterion is written out plainly: 'The predicted critical temperatures ... are taken as temperatures at which the network is maximally confused, i.e., when the average output crosses 0.5', and 'the network is maximally confused (average is 0.5) at the transition temperatures'. Practical detail worth quoting in a book: because the averaged output is noisy, they fit a third-degree polynomial to the data near the 0.5 crossing to locate it. The physical setting is a three-dimensional convolutional network trained on determinantal-quantum-Monte-Carlo auxiliary-field configurations of the 3D Hubbard model (spatial 4^3 or 8^3 sites, 200 imaginary-time slices, 32/16/8 feature maps, dropout 0.5, softmax readout), which reproduces the Neel phase boundary at half filling and is then TRANSFER-LEARNED into the sign-problematic doped region, predicting magnetic order out to at least 5% doping.
verifiedClaims.people: Kelvin Ch'ng; Juan Carrasquilla; Roger G. Melko; Ehsan Khatami
verifiedClaims.affiliation: San Jose State University (Ch'ng, Khatami); Perimeter Institute and University of Waterloo (Carrasquilla, Melko)

verifiedClaims.claim: INTERPRETABLE KERNEL METHODS - THE DECISION FUNCTION IS m^2, AND THE GAUGE THEORY NEEDS DEGREE FOUR. Ponte and Melko replace neural networks with support vector machines using polynomial kernels K(sigma,sigma') = (sigma . sigma' + c_0)^k, so the decision function can be written down explicitly. For the 2D Ising model at T from 1.6 to 2.9: the linear kernel k = 1 fails outright (a linear boundary cannot separate three clusters, and its learned coefficients are structureless random numbers), while the quadratic kernel k = 2 reaches about 97% mean test accuracy at L = 40 with only a few dozen training samples, and its decision function d(sigma), plotted against temperature, coincides with the squared magnetization per spin m^2 = (sum_a sigma_a / N)^2 after fixing an overall scale and offset. For the conserved-order-parameter Ising model the quadratic SVM's coefficient map reproduces Wang's analytic structure factor. For the 2D Ising gauge theory at T = 0 versus T = infinity: EVERY polynomial kernel of degree less than 4 gives about 50% accuracy - pure guessing - while degree 4 converges to 100%, showing the classifier must literally reconstruct the four-spin plaquette term of the Hamiltonian to evaluate whether the local constraints are satisfied. Larger L needs more training samples to find that decision function.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, and Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics

verifiedClaims.claim: THE KOSTERLITZ-THOULESS CASE: THE NETWORK CHEATS WITH THE MAGNETIZATION. Beach, Golubeva and Melko ask whether a network can classify phases from TOPOLOGICAL DEFECTS rather than a bulk order parameter, using the 2D classical XY model. Findings: a single-layer network does NOT correctly classify the phases of the XY model; a convolutional network classifies easily, but it does so 'by learning the global magnetization' - a finite-size pseudo-order-parameter, not the vortices; 'significant feature engineering of the raw spin states is required to convincingly claim that features of the vortex configurations are responsible for learning the transition temperature'. They then design a deep network that can learn vortices without feature engineering, and find that detecting vortices does not necessarily give the best classification accuracy, especially for lattices below roughly 1000 spins. This is the sharpest single demonstration that high classification accuracy is not evidence that the network has found the physically correct mechanism.
verifiedClaims.people: Matthew J. S. Beach; Anna Golubeva; Roger G. Melko
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo; Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics (Melko)

verifiedClaims.claim: THE ONE-HALF CROSSING IS NOT A RELIABLE ESTIMATOR IN GENERAL. Chertenkov, Burovski and Shchur redo the supervised classification for two models in two universality classes - the 2D Ising model and the 2D Baxter-Wu model - across six architectures: a fully connected network, a CNN, and ResNet-10/18/34/50. They confirm the Carrasquilla-Melko phenomenology (output near 1 at low T, near 0 at high T, transition region narrowing with L) but find that the equal-prediction point F^T = 1/2 is systematically shifted into the paramagnetic phase for the fully connected network at all lattice sizes for both models, and shifted non-systematically for the ResNets (for ResNet-50 on the Ising model, L = 96, 144, 216 shift one way and L = 48, 72 the other). Their explicit conclusion: 'F^T = 1/2 is not a reliable finite-size estimate of the critical temperature T_c, in general'; it happens to work for a CNN on Ising data, which is the Carrasquilla-Melko case. They propose instead the VARIANCE of the network output function, whose peak sits in the critical region and whose peak WIDTH obeys finite-size scaling governed by nu, and extract T_c to within one standard error using a Ferdinand-Fisher fit (e.g. FCNN 2.2691(4), CNN 2.2687(4) for Ising).
verifiedClaims.people: Vladislav Chertenkov; Evgeni Burovski; Lev Shchur
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics, Chernogolovka; HSE University, Moscow

verifiedClaims.claim: WHAT THESE NETWORKS CONVERGE TO, ANALYTICALLY. Arnold and Schaefer derive closed-form expressions for the OPTIMAL output of three widely used neural-network methods for detecting phase transitions - including the Carrasquilla-Melko supervised scheme and the van Nieuwenburg learning-by-confusion scheme - in the limit of infinite model capacity, i.e. what a sufficiently large, well-trained network is approximating. The optimal predictions depend explicitly on the underlying data distributions, which is what reveals 'the inner workings of the considered methods'. Practically, evaluating the analytic expressions locates phase transitions directly from experimentally accessible data with no network training at all, and is faster. Validated numerically on topological, quantum, and many-body-localization transitions. This is the paper to cite when a book wants to say what the classifier is 'really' computing rather than what it happens to have learned.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Basel; CSAIL and Department of Mathematics, MIT (Schaefer)

verifiedClaims.claim: THE OTHER CONTEMPORANEOUS CNN PAPER, OFTEN OMITTED. Tanaka and Tomiya trained a CNN on 2D Ising configurations labelled by DISCRETIZED INVERSE TEMPERATURE (not by phase), showed it finds the feature of the phase transition with no a priori information about it, defined a new order parameter constructed from the CNN itself that yields a well-approximated critical inverse temperature consistent with the exact value, and found empirically that the ReLU activation in the convolution layer is important for detecting the transition. This is the paper Kashiwa, Kikuchi and Tomiya later dissect; it establishes the temperature-regression variant of the protocol alongside the Carrasquilla-Melko phase-classification variant.
verifiedClaims.affiliation: RIKEN (Tanaka); Central China Normal University / RIKEN BNL (Tomiya)

verifiedClaims.claim: THE PROTOCOL RUN ON REAL EXPERIMENTAL DATA. Rem, Kaeming, Tarnowski, Asteria, Flaeschner, Becker, Sengstock and Weitenberg applied artificial neural networks to single-shot momentum-space density images from ultracold-atom experiments rather than to Monte Carlo configurations, mapping out the two-dimensional topological phase diagram of the Haldane model and characterizing the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition in an inhomogeneous Bose-Hubbard system. Useful as the endpoint of the chapter's arc: the same supervised-classification idea, with experimental images as the raw configurations.
verifiedClaims.people: Benno S. Rem; Niklas Kaeming; Matthias Tarnowski; Luca Asteria; Nick Flaeschner; Christoph Becker; Klaus Sengstock; Christof Weitenberg
